newsitem.title: CHINA: Manulife sees Shanghai JV profit in 7 years.
newsitem.headline: Manulife sees Shanghai JV profit in 7 years.

text.p: Manulife Financial of Canada's new life insurance joint venture in Shanghai should turn a profit after seven years, company president and chief executive officer Dominic D'Alessandro said in an interview.
He also said he expected China to approve one new joint venture with a foreign firm in the life insurance field each year.

Zhong Hong Life Insurance is a joint venture between Manulife (International) Ltd, a wholly owned subsidiary of Manulife Financial, Canada's largest insurance company, and China Trust and Investment Corporation for Foreign Economic Relations and Trade (FOTIC), a member of the Sinochem group.
It is China's first joint-venture life insurance company. The firm officially opened for business on Tuesday.

"In roughly seven years' time, this venture will be self-sustaining and profitable," D'Allesandro said, adding that insurance companies take longer to make a profit than other businesses. "We are not looking for explosive growth."

Zhong Hong has a licence to sell in the greater Shanghai area and plans, subject to approval by the People's Bank of China (PBOC), to start with personal accident and health products, adding endowment and life policies later.
D'Alessandro declined to make income projections but said Zhong Hong expected to have 400 to 500 full-time agents within a year, targeting sales at the city's growing middle class.
Life-insurance policies will cost about 1,500 yuan ($181) a year while personal accident policies will fetch 700-800 yuan, he said.
The average Shanghai worker earned 9,242 yuan in annual income in 1995, official figures show.

Manulife is the second foreign insurer to enter the Chinese life-insurance market after American International Assurance (AIA), a member of the American International Group, which operates without a local partner.
Tokio Marine and Fire Insurance and Wintherthur WINZ.Z have been given licences to handle non-life policies.
D'Alessandro said his company would have preferred a wholly owned venture but, with the exception of AIA, foreign life insurers in China must operate through joint-venture partners.
It took 18 months from the time Manulife was told it had won a licence to find a joint venture partner, negotiate an agreement and get it approved by the PBOC, the central bank.
"The administrative environment for the insurance industry is changing very quickly," said Victor Apps, chief executive officer of Manulife (International).
"A few years ago there were virtually no regulations at all surrounding the insurance industry. It makes it unpredictable what is going to happen in the next few years," he said.
